welcome.title: Take the guided tour?

menu.title: Deep Dives

step0.title: Welcome, let's take the tour
step0.description:
🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. Leave whenever — click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is one model that holds your data, its metadata and the processing between them. The same model defines your data estate and operates it — it is all one thing, and it stays out of the data path.

That is why everything stays in sync, and why reuse is built in: a relationship, metric, mask or rule defined once serves every surface, environment and role. Duplicate tables and metrics, duplicate commands and rules, even two systems serving the same data sit side by side in the model, so duplication is easy to see and simple to remove.

It is compact, extensible and composable. It slots in beside what you have, brings order to the sprawl, and lets every data professional apply their expertise without limiting their imagination — it only removes the drudgery.

🎯 The core is one short exercise: connect a database, then query it in the language or tool you already use — or just ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop, with no infrastructure to stand up.

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCPPostgres · pgwireNeo4j · BoltJDBC · Java/JVMArrow Flight SQL · ADBCDuckDB · airport

Everything after that is a Deep Dive you pick from a menu when you are ready.

Ready? Let's connect a source. →

stepPolly.title: Meet Polly, your setup assistant
stepPolly.description:
💬 Polly sets Provisa up in plain language — much easier than reading the docs.

“register my Postgres” · “fake the email column in the customers table” · “create a QA environment on synthetic data” · “who can see salaries?”

Polly works through the same governed APIs and rights as the UI, so it can only do what you can. Polly is open here; the chat button reopens this panel anytime.

step1.title: Start with Sources
step1.description:
Everything you want to federate is registered here:
🗄️ Databases🏢 Warehouses🔌 APIs📄 Files☁️ SaaS

Provisa unifies them all into one queryable graph.

step2.title: Register a source
step2.description: ➕ New connections start with this button — PostgreSQL, Snowflake, MongoDB, a REST API, a CSV, and 50+ more.

step3.title: 72 source types, 14 categories
step3.description:
One picker lists every type, grouped by category: Subscriptions, RDBMS, Cloud DW, Analytics, Data Lake, NoSQL, Code, Graph, File, API, Streaming, Enterprise, Data Quality, Other. Search by name or alias, or narrow with the category chips. Each type shows its logo and a reach icon: ⚡ read live in place, or a copy icon where Provisa reads a refreshed replica.

Pick one, fill the connection, Save.

step4.title: Everything becomes a table
step4.description:
Whatever the source — a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint, a graph — Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.

step5.title: Pick columns & policy
step5.description:
Choose a source, schema, and table, then pick columns — each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking — redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility — show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases — rename for the model

That's the whole setup — a source and a few tables. 🚀 Now let's query it. →

stepQuery.title: Query it your way
stepQuery.description: 💬 You ask in the language or tool you already use — SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, plain language through Polly, or a BI tool or driver — and every one reads the same governed model, so the answer and the rules are the same whichever you pick.

step6.title: SQL (1 of 7 surfaces)
step6.description:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source — join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. And the model's own metadata and every activity trace are themselves queryable tables here — join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 Not just this explorer — the same governed SQL runs through multiple wire protocols; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire — every Postgres-compatible client — psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI — connects out of the box.
  • JDBC — drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline, or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL — columnar streaming for ADBC clients — no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport — ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.

step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 7 surfaces)
step7.description:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

Grouping and aggregates over your relationships — 🎯 one endpoint, 📖 self-documenting schema.

🔌 Hit it from any GraphQL client — Apollo, Relay, urql — and, with federation enabled, drop Provisa into an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.

step8.title: Cypher (3 of 7 surfaces)
step8.description:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources — no single graph database required.

🔌 And any Bolt client — Neo4j Browser, Bloom — runs that same traversal over the wire, no code change.

step9.title: gRPC (4 of 7 surfaces)
step9.description:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Call it from any gRPC client — 📐 strongly typed, 🚀 high-throughput.

step10.title: JSON:API (5 of 7 surfaces)
step10.description:
🧩 A spec-compliant JSON:API surface:

GET /data/jsonapi/pet-store/inquiries?page[size]=20

📄 Paging and 🔍 filtering out of the box.

step11.title: OpenAPI / REST (6 of 7 surfaces)
step11.description:
🌐 And a plain REST endpoint, described by OpenAPI:

GET /data/rest/pet-store/inquiries

📄 Fully described, so any REST client or code generator can consume it.

step12.title: MCP (7 of 7 surfaces)
step12.description:
🤖 The seventh surface lets an agent reason with your data. It drives the very same governed tools — search the catalog, describe tables, run SQL, follow relationships — and chains them to answer questions no single query could, every call bound by your role's governance.

🔌 The same MCP server plugs into Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or any MCP client, so agents explore and reason over your model the governed way.

🔑 Uses your own LLM key; this exchange is a canned example.

One surface left — the one that writes all seven for you. →

step13.title: Just ask — the surface that writes all seven
step13.description:
💬 "how many pets per species"

🎁 Here's the capstone: you don't have to learn any of those seven. Ask in plain English and Provisa compiles your question into every query language at once — each panel below is that one sentence as SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, gRPC, JSON:API, and REST.

Use the surface your tools already speak — or skip them all and just ask.

🔑 Live natural-language queries use your own LLM key; this one's a canned example.

✅ One model, eight surfaces — seven to query, and the one that writes them.

Natural LanguageSQLGraphQLCyphergRPCJSON:APIRESTMCP

step14.title: That's the five-minute core
step14.description:
✅ You just saw it end to end: one source, queried in the language or tool you already use — or just asked in plain English. That's the whole promise — and you could stop right here.

Everything else is a Deep Dive: connecting data, relationships, modeling, governance, querying, test data, publishing and operating. Done opens the Deep Dives catalog.

step15.title: Connect the graph
step15.description:
A relationship does two jobs. It shapes your data model: how tables across sources and domains connect — which is what every query surface follows, whether GraphQL nesting, Cypher paths or SQL joins.

It is also a rule. Joins are governed: a role without the ignore_relationships right can join only along registered relationships, so which ones exist decides which queries are legal. Grant that right deliberately to a role you trust and it joins freely (never in high-security mode).

Relationships link tables across sources — even across different databases — turning flat tables into a traversable graph.

step16.title: Define a relationship
step16.description:
🔗 Map a source column to a target column and set cardinality:
1 → 11 → ∞∞ → ∞

✨ Or let Provisa infer relationships for you with AI.

🛡️ Because a relationship is a rule, adding, changing or removing one can make a query legal or illegal. A relationship requested from outside the source table's domain, or by someone who may not create relationships, waits for approval.

stepRelsSuggest.title: Suggest relationships
stepRelsSuggest.description: ✨ The sparkle button looks for likely joins: it reads the foreign keys your sources declare and, when an AI model key is configured, asks the model to infer more. Nothing is declared until you accept a candidate, and a rejected one stays out until you clear the rejections.

stepRelsList.title: Every relationship in one list
stepRelsList.description: 📋 The model's relationships, whether or not a source declares them, filterable and sortable. Expand a row to edit it or add its reverse. A role joins only along these relationships unless it holds the ignore_relationships right.

step17.title: See the ERD
step17.description: The entity-relationship diagram renders your whole federated model — every registered table and the relationships between them.

step18.title: Access control (RBAC)
step18.description:
🔐 Registering a table sets per-column access, wired straight into roles:
👁️ Read✏️ Write

That's role-based access control — and the roles themselves are defined here on the Security page.

stepRoleInherit.title: Roles inherit
stepRoleInherit.description: 👪 A role can inherit from a parent: it receives the parent's grants, column visibility and row rules, and its own row rule for a table replaces the parent's. The role also carries its capabilities and its rate and complexity limits.

step19.title: Row-level security
step19.description:
🔎 Once roles exist, go finer — restrict which rows each role sees with attribute-based predicates:

region = user.region AND status != 'archived'

📐 Data-driven and enforced per row — across every source and protocol.

stepDomains.title: Domains and their stewards
stepDomains.description: 🗂️ A domain groups tables, and its data steward governs that part of the model: who sees what, masks and row rules, sensitive data, and its glossary and data products.

stepTags.title: Tags carry meaning
stepTags.description: 🏷️ A tag is one org-wide label with a fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships or commands. Tags carry behavior, not only documentation, and a tag can require a reason, an expiry date or a parameter when it is applied.

stepRequests.title: Relationship requests
stepRequests.description: ✋ This request comes from someone who may not create relationships themselves, often from outside your domain, wanting to relate their tables to yours — usually the first step toward asking for your data. Relationships are governed, so approving one changes which queries are legal: a role that may join only along approved relationships can now join across it. A relationship request needs two approvals before it can be executed. A relationship across two domains needs a yes from each side. Approve it, execute it, or reject it with a reason from a fixed list; resolved requests move to the Resolved tab.

stepQualityTable.title: A quality checker is just a source
stepQualityTable.description: 🧪 A data-quality checker — Soda or Great Expectations — registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.

stepQualityPanel.title: Build a quality contract
stepQualityPanel.description: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column — null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness — and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.

stepQualityProfile.title: Profile a table
stepQualityProfile.description: 📊 A table joins a Data Profiler on its editor's Quality tab, a source that profiles its member tables on a schedule. A run measures each column's shape, distributions and value frequencies, and the children per parent. Run Profile Now starts one and View Profile Runs reads them. Results land as tables you register and govern like any other; until you register them, no reader sees a profile. The next card puts checks on them.

stepProfilerChecks.title: Checks on profile results
stepProfilerChecks.description: Every run adds rows to its result tables: columns (null share, distinct count, range), runs (row count), children per parent, quantiles and drift. Register a result table and a data-quality checker, a Soda or Great Expectations source like any other, can scan it, so any measure a profile produces can carry a check that raises an issue. Drift is one such measure: each run is compared with the table's recent runs, and a measure that moves is flagged. An accepted constraint, a drift check, or a check against expectations from outside Provisa can be added to the checker's contract from the profiler's runs.

stepQualityProduct.title: Quality travels with the product
stepQualityProduct.description: ✅ A product's Data Quality panel lists the checker tables whose contracts scan its output ports, so a consumer sees the evidence next to the product. It is empty until a checker scans one. Data products are published in the Publish it Deep Dive.

stepTestDataMap.title: How the parts fit
stepTestDataMap.description:
Safe, realistic data to build and test against comes from four parts, each with one job:

  • Environment: a branch of the model. At creation it inherits its parent's connections or starts unbound, and you point its sources at your own databases.
  • Profiler: measures real tables, giving the shapes everything else is built from.
  • Fakes: in test data, a column's fake replaces its identifying values.
  • Synthetic data: fills a non-production environment with generated rows shaped like the profiled tables.

stepTestDataProfiler.title: What fakes and synthetic data are built from
stepTestDataProfiler.description: 📊 A Data Profiler measures the tables you add to it: column shapes, distributions, value frequencies and children per parent. Fill from profile turns those measures into fakes, and a synthetic dataset draws its rows from them. Watching the same runs for drift is covered in the Data quality Deep Dive.

stepFakes.title: Declare a fake
stepFakes.description: 🎭 The Testing tab of a table's Columns shows each column's fake, such as email(). Fake only the identifying columns and keep the rest real. A column can also carry a synthetic rule, used only when generating synthetic data.

stepFakesFill.title: Fill fakes from a profile
stepFakesFill.description: ✨ Fill from profile proposes fakes for identifying columns, and synthetic rules for the rest, from the table's latest profile. Nothing saves until you save the form.

stepEnvKinds.title: Environments and their connections
stepEnvKinds.description: An environment is a branch of your model, and the list shows which one each was made from. When you create one, Inherit connections reads that environment's source connections by reference, so a rotation there is picked up here. Leave it off, the default, to get the whole model with none of the connections, and point each source at your own database.

stepSynthetic.title: Generate synthetic data
stepSynthetic.description: 🧪 In the Synthetic data tab, define a dataset from the profile runs of the tables you name and press Generate. It fills a non-production environment with rows shaped like those tables, with the same relationships and fan-out, at the scale you choose. A comparison report shows how close it came.

stepSyntheticPrivacy.title: Private by design
stepSyntheticPrivacy.description: 🔒 Declare a dataset private with a privacy budget ε. Calibrated noise is added to every statistic the generator draws from a profile, and the report states what the noise dropped.

step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
step20.description:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here — no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views — over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands — governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data — invokable from every surface, fully governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts — declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics — governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once; every surface — SQL, GraphQL, AI agents — computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.

step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
step21.description:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars — recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar, not just a clock.
  • 🗄️ Store As… — replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel — bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.

stepMetrics.title: Metrics, defined once
stepMetrics.description: 📏 A metric is the business definition of a measure, an aggregate over one fact table. Define it once and SQL, GraphQL, the explore canvas and every view built from it compute the same number; a view regenerates when its metric changes.

stepCommands.title: Commands
stepCommands.description: ⚡ A command is a governed, typed operation, such as an HTTP service, a Python model or a stored procedure. Register it once and call it from every surface, with the same rights and tracing as a query.

step22.title: Lineage, end to end
step22.description:
🧬 Lineage is the dependency trail your derivations leave: what each view, calculated column or metric is built from, and what depends on it. This is a real query, analyzed — follow name_upper back through its transforms to the exact source columns that feed it.

Nothing runs — the query is only analyzed.

stepObservability.title: Traces and debug tracing
stepObservability.description: 🔭 Tracing records one span per request. The Debug tracing tab adds a span per pipeline stage and per source call, with SQL text. It adds load, so turn it on for one org, role or source for a set time; it turns itself off when the time is up.

stepCache.title: Caches and replicas
stepCache.description: 🗄️ These layers are separate. The response cache holds query results, and a request opts in with @cached or a SQL comment. Small lookup tables are mirrored to speed joins. A replica of a source table that cannot be attached lives in the durable store, beside materialized views.

stepScheduled.title: Triggers
stepScheduled.description: ⏱️ Run a webhook, a SQL statement or a command on a cron schedule, when a table changes, or on a table's error or quarantine. A trigger runs as a role you choose, so governance applies, and each shows how its last run ended.

step23.title: Operate it
step23.description:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine — pluggable: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime — the model, the surfaces, and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach — Parquet, Iceberg, Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials auto-provisioned. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability — redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management
  • 📤 Export the model's configuration — the whole model or chosen sections — as a file to review, diff and ship through CI/CD

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step — no rewrite:

  • Develop — embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale — Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote — point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.

stepPreview.title: Preview any table
stepPreview.description: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview — live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.

stepReports.title: Management reports, built in
stepReports.description: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports — usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health — each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.

stepProductForm.title: Define a data product
stepProductForm.description: 📦 Name the owner and team, the purpose, usage, SLA and support, then pick the tables and commands it contains. These are the fields that get published. A table joins a product only when both share the same domain.

stepGlossary.title: A living business glossary
stepGlossary.description: 📖 Every term links to the columns that carry it and to other terms — curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps: ✨ Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and ✨ Relationships proposes links across the whole glossary. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.

stepDataProducts.title: Data products, published where consumers already look
stepDataProducts.description:
📦 Every product here speaks ODPS (the Open Data Product Standard) — owner, team, purpose, limitations, usage, SLA, support, custom properties — and Provisa auto-publishes it straight into Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex, so it shows up as a native product in the catalog your consumers already use.

🔁 There's no separate export step to forget: the spec is derived from the live model — tables, lineage, tags, glossary terms — every time, so what's published can't drift out of date the way a hand-maintained ODPS file would.

✅ Publishing also sends an ontology extract: the part of your glossary that bears on what is published — the terms that define its columns, the broader and related terms they connect to, and the typed relationships between them. The data-quality results of the checkers that scan it go with it. A product's Related Terms panel lists its terms.

stepGlossaryTerm.title: Add a term
stepGlossaryTerm.description: 📖 A term names one business concept, lists the columns that carry it, links to the terms it relates to and says what it means. Terms for real columns are derived for you; add one by hand for a concept no single column carries.

stepPublish.title: Publish to the tools your org uses
stepPublish.description:
📤 Publish it where your org already looks. Catalog entries (tables, columns, domains, stewards, approved relationships), data products and column-level lineage go out, and each target receives what it supports: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Collibra, Atlan and Apache Atlas as catalogs, Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex as data-product listings, and lineage over OpenLineage.

Publication is outbound only: Provisa never reads a target back as a source of truth.

stepRelsAgents.title: Relationships and AI agents
stepRelsAgents.description:
🤖 The model and its relationships are available to AI agents — Polly, and agents connecting over MCP — and they shape the queries those agents write.

An agent runs under a role, so the same rule applies to it as to a person: a query that joins outside the registered relationships fails. This is enforced, not advisory.

It is also your choice. To let an agent discover relationships, grant its role the ignore_relationships right; to keep it inside guardrails, leave the role without it. It is the same deliberate grant as for a trusted identity (never honored in high-security mode).

weblogsSources.title: What this demo is
weblogsSources.description: A small web shop wants to know which pages are slow, and which SQL makes them slow. The answer is split across nginx's access log, the database's statement log and the shop's own database. The tour shows how Provisa reads log files as tables, joins them across sources and governs them by role, then answers the question in SQL and over REST.

weblogsLogFiles.title: Three sources
weblogsLogFiles.description: The shop has three sources: shop-db, its PostgreSQL database, and two log sources, shop_access and shop_db_log. Provisa reads each log file where it sits, one line to a row, and again every 30 seconds; nothing is loaded or copied first.

weblogsTables.title: Sources become tables
weblogsTables.description: Each source's data is registered as tables: the shop's customers, products and orders, and one table for each log, its lines split into columns such as path, status and time. Views, saved queries over them, add the slowest pages and the SQL each request ran.

weblogsJoin.title: One request, two logs
weblogsJoin.description: nginx gives every request an id, and the shop names each database connection after it. The LOGGED_FOR relationship tells Provisa to join a statement to its request on that id, so no query has to spell out the join.

weblogsRest.title: The same question over REST
weblogsRest.description: The slowest pages again, as a REST call: each path with its request count and its average and longest time. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed model, so REST gives the answer SQL or GraphQL would, under the same rights.

weblogsDone.title: What you just saw
weblogsDone.description: Three sources became tables, joined on a request id, and answered the shop's question in SQL and over REST.

sonnetsIntro.title: Shakespeare's sonnets, by meaning
sonnetsIntro.description: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets in Postgres, embedded into Qdrant, searched by meaning, grown into a graph. The question: which themes run through the sonnets, and where does Shakespeare echo himself? sonnets is the Postgres source, a row for each sonnet and for each of its 2,155 lines.

sonnetsVectors.title: The vector store
sonnetsVectors.description: vectors is Qdrant. It holds a point for each line, its vector the embedding of the line's words, and Provisa reads and writes it as it does any other source.

sonnetsLines.title: Every line, embedded
sonnetsLines.description: The line table holds a row for each of the 2,155 lines. The command embed_lines is one governed SQL statement: its embed() turns each line's words into a vector, and the rows are written to Qdrant through the collection's write route.

sonnetsSearch.title: A search by meaning
sonnetsSearch.description: lines_like is a search table: Provisa reads it live in Qdrant under the arguments the statement gives it, here a phrase and how many lines to find. Look at each line's score: how near it is to the phrase.

sonnetsThemeView.title: A theme, stored
sonnetsThemeView.description: Each theme view stores one fixed search, joined back to the lines it found, with each line's score. This one holds the twenty lines nearest to "the ravages of time"; four more hold beauty, mortality, jealousy and verse that outlives death.

sonnetsEchoes.title: Lines that echo each other
sonnetsEchoes.description: The echo table. The command link_echoes asks the vector store for each line's three nearest lines in other sonnets and writes them here, each with its similarity.

sonnetsGraph.title: A graph of the sonnets
sonnetsGraph.description: Three relationships make the tables a graph: a line is IN its sonnet, EVOKES a theme and ECHOES a line of another sonnet, with its score. Cypher walks them like any graph.

sonnetsEchoNetwork.title: The echo network
sonnetsEchoNetwork.description: The echo network, drawn by Cypher: the lines that closely echo a line of another sonnet, and the sonnets they are in. Look for the sonnets joined by more than one echo.

sonnetsThemesBySequence.title: Themes in the two sequences
sonnetsThemesBySequence.description: For each theme, how many of the lines it found are in the Fair Youth sonnets and how many in the Dark Lady sonnets. Look for a theme that belongs to one sequence.

sonnetsDone.title: From rows to a graph
sonnetsDone.description: Shakespeare's lines went from Postgres rows to Qdrant vectors, governed searches and a graph of echoes and themes.

weblogsStatements.title: The SQL behind a slow page
weblogsStatements.description: The slowest pages joined to the statements their requests ran, in plain SQL over two of the demo's views. A view is a saved query that Provisa expands into this statement before it runs. Here is where the time went, statement by statement.

filesIntro.title: An instant data lake
filesIntro.description: A city publishes its open data as files: 311 complaints in a CSV file a month, building permits in Parquet, the budget in Excel and inspections in JSON. drop is one files source over that folder: every file is a table, read where it lies, with no load step. The question: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?

filesComplaints.title: One table over many files
filesComplaints.description: complaints is one table over every file named complaints_*.csv in the folder. Each month's file is part of it; a new month's file needs no table of its own.

filesMonths.title: Rows from every file
filesMonths.description: The complaints counted by month: each month comes from its own file, read as one table. Look for one row for each monthly file.

filesFormats.title: A file of each format
filesFormats.description: building_permits is read from a Parquet file, as the budget is from an Excel workbook and the inspections from a JSON file. Each is a governed table like any other.

filesJoin.title: Complaints at permitted addresses
filesJoin.description: The relationship DRAWS joins a building permit to the complaints made at its address. The view that answers the question joins along it.

filesTerm.title: What an open complaint is
filesTerm.description: The glossary says what an open complaint is: one the city has not yet closed. Terms like this say what the catalog's data means.

filesAnswer.title: The answer
filesAnswer.description: The stored view complaints_near_construction counts, for each neighborhood, the complaints made at an address with an active permit. Look at which neighborhood comes first.

filesRest.title: The same answer over REST
filesRest.description: The same view as a REST call. Every table and view is served over REST, GraphQL and SQL alike, under the same rules.

filesDone.title: A folder became a catalog
filesDone.description: A folder of files became a governed catalog: tables, relationships, a glossary term and a stored view, with nothing loaded. A new month's complaints file needs no new table: the glob already names it.

reviewsCatalog.title: What this demo is
reviewsCatalog.description: An electronics shop wants to know which products disappoint, and what their buyers do about it. The answer is spread over three NoSQL stores. This one, catalog, is MongoDB: a document for each product, its specs nested, and the star ratings customers give.

reviewsSearchStore.title: The reviews, in Elasticsearch
reviewsSearchStore.description: reviews is Elasticsearch: the 5,000 reviews customers wrote, each with its product, its stars and its text. Provisa reads it live; nothing is copied first.

reviewsGraphStore.title: Who bought what, in Neo4j
reviewsGraphStore.description: purchases is Neo4j: 2,000 customers, each linked by a BOUGHT relationship to the products they bought. All three stores name a product by the same id.

reviewsPipeline.title: A MongoDB pipeline as a table
reviewsPipeline.description: ratings_by_product is a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, registered as a table: it groups the star ratings by product and gives each product's count, average and one-star ratings. A query reads it like any other table.

reviewsSearchTable.title: An Elasticsearch search as a table
reviewsSearchTable.description: reviews_matching is an Elasticsearch search, registered as a table. Its phrase is a parameter: a query sets it, and each row is a review whose text holds the phrase, with the phrase highlighted.

reviewsCypherTable.title: A Cypher query as a table
reviewsCypherTable.description: bought_together is a Cypher query against Neo4j, registered as a table: for each product, every other product its buyers bought, and how many of them did.

reviewsJoin.title: Joined on the product
reviewsJoin.description: Relationships join the tables on the product id across all three stores. COMPLAINS_ABOUT joins a matching review to its product in the catalog, so a query reaches from Elasticsearch to MongoDB without spelling out the join.

reviewsBatteryDies.title: Where the battery dies
reviewsBatteryDies.description: The shop's first question, in SQL: the reviews that say "battery dies", counted by product, with each product's ratings. One statement reads an Elasticsearch search and two MongoDB tables, and a handful of products stand out.

reviewsBoughtWith.title: What their buyers bought
reviewsBoughtWith.description: The second question, in Cypher: the products rated under three stars, and what their buyers also bought. The graph runs across the MongoDB ratings and the Neo4j purchases, and power banks keep turning up.

reviewsRest.title: The search over REST
reviewsRest.description: The same search as a REST call, its phrase passed as a parameter. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed tables, so REST answers as SQL and GraphQL do, under the same rights.

reviewsExample.title: The search in GraphQL
reviewsExample.description: An example query: the battery complaints in GraphQL, each review's highlighted text with its product nested beneath it through the relationship.

reviewsDone.title: What you just saw
reviewsDone.description: Three NoSQL stores, a MongoDB pipeline, an Elasticsearch search and a Cypher query, joined on the product and asked the shop's question in SQL, Cypher, REST and GraphQL.

insuranceScenario.title: What this demo is
insuranceScenario.description: A property insurer wants to know where its exposure is concentrated against natural-hazard risk. Its own book of policies, with the total insured value of each, is in its database; the hazard risk of every US county is public, in FEMA's, the US Forest Service's and NOAA's data. The tour shows Provisa joining the two, by county, and answering the question in SQL, over REST and in GraphQL.

insuranceJoin.title: Joined by county
insuranceJoin.description: The book and the public risk tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.

insuranceAnswer.title: The answer in SQL
insuranceAnswer.description: The view exposure_by_county joins the book to the risk in each county, and is kept stored. Ordered by insured value weighted by risk percentile, it puts the counties where the most exposure meets the highest risk first.

insuranceRecap.title: What you saw
insuranceRecap.description: The insurer's own data, read live, and public risk data, landed once, joined by county in one governed model: one view answers where the exposure meets the risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, under each role's access.

insuranceGovdata.title: The public risk data
insuranceGovdata.description: The government data comes from AskAmerica, a live account. Its three county tables are landed once, when the demo is built, and read from that copy for good: they never expire, and this demo never calls the account.

insuranceBook.title: The insurer's book
insuranceBook.description: Each policy in force, read live from the insurer's own database: its county, line of business, total insured value, premium and deductible.

insuranceRisk.title: FEMA's National Risk Index
insuranceRisk.description: Every US county's all-hazard risk score and rating, its national percentile, its expected annual loss and the value of all its buildings. The wildfire and storm tables sit beside it.

insuranceTerms.title: In the insurer's terms
insuranceTerms.description: The glossary names what an underwriter asks about: total insured value, accumulation, probable maximum loss, expected annual loss. Here accumulation: exposure concentrated where one event reaches many policies.

insuranceByRating.title: By risk rating, in GraphQL
insuranceByRating.description: The same view grouped by FEMA's risk rating: how much of the book's insured value sits in counties rated Relatively High or Very High.

insuranceRest.title: The same answer over REST
insuranceRest.description: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.

qualityIntro.title: Data you can trust
qualityIntro.description: A chain of five shops sends its sales as a feed, a batch a day, landed as bronze into sales, the chain's database. Everything after bronze is a materialized view: the checks, silver and gold, refreshed by landing alone. The question: can I trust this data before it reaches gold?

qualityBronze.title: Bronze: typed where it is clean
qualityBronze.description: bronze holds every batch as it landed, never changed. Clean data is typed on landing: the sale id, when it was sold, the quantity. The messy fields, shop code, product and price, stay raw until silver. Its probe watches it, so a new batch refreshes every view after it.

qualityRaw.title: Raw, as the feed spelled it
qualityRaw.description: The products of the first batch as they landed: one product in several spellings, such as COFFEE, Coffee and cofee. Silver makes them one.

qualityChecks.title: The checks, on every batch
qualityChecks.description: dq_results is a materialized view that computes the checks in SQL on every landed batch: how many rows fail each, and pass or fail. Batch 1 passes them all; batch 2 fails three.

qualityAdmitted.title: From a row to the checks that admitted it
qualityAdmitted.description: Every silver row carries the run id of the checks that admitted its batch. The relationship ADMITTED_BY joins it to those checks in dq_results.

qualityWhichChecks.title: Which checks admitted silver
qualityWhichChecks.description: A silver sale and, along ADMITTED_BY, every check of the run that admitted it: each one passed, with no failing rows.

qualityRefused.title: What the bad batch failed on
qualityRefused.description: The rows of batch 2 that fail a check, still in bronze as they landed: a shop the chain does not have, negative quantities, prices that are not numbers. None of batch 2 reaches silver; batch 1 stays.

qualitySilver.title: Silver: cleaned
qualitySilver.description: Silver is bronze cleaned, from the passing batches only: shop codes trimmed and upper-cased, one spelling a product, the price a number, the day derived, and a sale sent twice kept once, at its latest.

qualityGold.title: Gold: the totals
qualityGold.description: Gold is one GROUP BY over silver: sales, items, revenue and the price range by day and product, from checked data only.

qualityDone.title: Trust you can query
qualityDone.description: Landing a batch refreshed the checks, silver and gold, with nothing else run. The clean batch reached gold; the bad one stopped at bronze, and why is a query.

insiderIntro.title: Insider review at a bank
insiderIntro.description: Northgate Partners, an invented bank, keeps a watch list of the deals it is working on. The question: is anyone sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank? bank is its database: the watch list, the employees and their mail, and the customers and who read their records. Every name and record here is generated.

insiderWatchList.title: The watch list
insiderWatchList.description: deal is the control room's watch list: each deal's company, the names it goes by, its ticker, its project code name and whether it is public yet. It is the most restricted table here: the control room reads it, a deal team only its own deal, and a first-level reviewer never.

insiderMail.title: The mail
insiderMail.description: message holds the employees' outbound mail: who sent it, when, and how many recipients were outside the bank or at a personal address.

insiderMatch.title: Every message against every deal
insiderMatch.description: deal_match is what the match_deals command found: for each message and deal, whether it names the company, an alias, the ticker or the code name, and how close it reads to the deal's description through a local embedding model. A paraphrase that avoids every name still scores.

insiderQueue.title: The review queue
insiderQueue.description: One materialized view ranks every case. The match is weighted by context: a sender outside the deal's team, a recipient outside the bank or at a personal address, and a message sent before the announcement raise it; a deal-team member writing to the deal's own counterparties lowers it.

insiderLeak.title: A paraphrase outranks the expected mail
insiderLeak.description: Two of the messages behind the queue. A trader not on deal Falcon tells a personal address about it in his own words, with no name, ticker or code name, and it ranks near the top. The deal team's mail to the deal's counsel names everything, and ranks low.

insiderCustomerData.title: Customer data
insiderCustomerData.description: The same mail is checked for customer data by SQL patterns: social security and account numbers. The customer table's columns are tagged pii, so this read is itself recorded.

insiderPiiAccess.title: Who read customer data
insiderPiiAccess.description: ops.pii_access lists every read of a pii-tagged table: here, the read you just made. The queue does the same for the bank's staff from the bank's own access log: the operations employee who read customer records that week and then mailed customer data out ranks first.

insiderAsReviewer.title: As a first-level reviewer
insiderAsReviewer.description: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer_ben, the first-level reviewer of the trading, research and operations desks.

insiderReviewerQueue.title: Only their own cases
insiderReviewerQueue.description: The same queue, read as the reviewer: only the cases of the desks they review, the flagged entity shown and the deal withheld. Row rules on the mail and its matches do this; nothing is copied. The watch list itself is refused to them.

insiderAsControlRoom.title: Back to the control room
insiderAsControlRoom.description: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.

insiderAudit.title: Every read is recorded
insiderAudit.description: ops.queries records every statement: who ran it, as which role, over which table. The reviewer's reads of the queue and the watch list are here, as are yours.

insiderWhyFlagged.title: Why was it flagged?
insiderWhyFlagged.description: Polly helps the human reviewer after the fact. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.

insiderOverTheWall.title: Was the sender over the wall?
insiderOverTheWall.description: Who was brought over the wall for the deal, and so who could have known of it. The flagged sender is not among them.

insiderDone.title: What this is, and is not
insiderDone.description: Watch-list deals were matched against outbound mail by name and by meaning, ranked for review, and the list itself was never shown to the reviewer. This is post-review analytics behind real-time controls, not a replacement for data-loss prevention. Attachments, images, encoded text and personal channels are outside it. Monitoring employees needs disclosure and, in places, a works-council agreement.

vulnerabilitiesScenario.title: What this demo is
vulnerabilitiesScenario.description: A software company wants to know which of the vulnerabilities in its code attackers actually exploit, and how long each has gone unfixed. Its repositories, their packages and the Dependabot alerts on them are in its own database; the CVE records and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities are public. The tour shows Provisa joining the two by CVE and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.

vulnerabilitiesGovdata.title: The public vulnerability data
vulnerabilitiesGovdata.description: The government data comes from AskAmerica, a live account: the NVD's CVE records, MITRE's catalog of software weaknesses and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities. Its tables are landed once, when the demo is built, and read from that copy for good: this demo never calls the account.

vulnerabilitiesAlerts.title: The Dependabot alerts
vulnerabilitiesAlerts.description: One alert for each pinned package version with a published advisory: the repository, the package, the CVE, the version that fixes it, and whether the alert is open, fixed or dismissed. It is read live from the company's database.

vulnerabilitiesNvd.title: The CVE records, landed through a filter
vulnerabilitiesNvd.description: The NVD holds a quarter of a million CVEs, and the company's alerts name nineteen. The table's landing filter, a condition on its own columns, keeps only those when the table is landed, so the copy holds just the records the alerts need.

vulnerabilitiesKev.title: CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities
vulnerabilitiesKev.description: Each CVE that attackers are known to exploit, with the date federal agencies must fix it by and whether ransomware campaigns use it. Landed whole: it is small.

vulnerabilitiesJoin.title: Exploited, by CVE
vulnerabilitiesJoin.description: A CVE record and its entry in CISA's catalog share the CVE identifier, and this relationship joins them. With the alerts joined to their CVEs, an alert reaches the catalog in two steps.

vulnerabilitiesTerms.title: The vocabulary
vulnerabilitiesTerms.description: Known exploited vulnerability, CVE, CWE and CVSS, in the company's glossary, each tied to the columns it is about. A CVSS score says how severe a vulnerability is; only the catalog says whether anyone exploits it.

vulnerabilitiesAnswer.title: The answer in SQL
vulnerabilitiesAnswer.description: The view exploited_in_our_code keeps each open alert whose CVE is in CISA's catalog, with the days since CISA's due date passed, and is kept stored. Internet-facing repositories first, longest overdue first: where to start.

vulnerabilitiesByTeam.title: The answer in GraphQL
vulnerabilitiesByTeam.description: The same view, grouped by team on the server: how many exploited vulnerabilities each team has open, and how long the oldest has been overdue.

vulnerabilitiesGraph.title: The answer as a graph
vulnerabilitiesGraph.description: The same joins as a graph in Cypher: repositories, the open alerts raised in them, their CVEs and the catalog entries that mark them exploited.

vulnerabilitiesRest.title: The same answer over REST
vulnerabilitiesRest.description: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and counted on the server. A ticketing system or a dashboard gets the answer without writing SQL.

vulnerabilitiesRecap.title: What you saw
vulnerabilitiesRecap.description: The company's own code data, read live, and public vulnerability data, landed once and only as much of it as the alerts need, joined by CVE in one governed model: one view answers which exploited vulnerabilities sit in the code and how overdue each is, in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.

testdataScenario.title: Can I test against realistic data without touching production?
testdataScenario.description: shop-db is a shop's production database: its customers, products and orders. Developers and testers need data of the same shape to work against, but the customers' names, emails and cities are personal data, and copies of production drift. The data here is itself generated, to stand in for a real shop.

testdataTables.title: Each column declares its fake
testdataTables.description: Every column of customers names the kind of value it holds, its fake: a person's name, an email address, a city, one of four regions, a date in a range. The model carries it with the column, so the fake is defined once, where the column is.

testdataJoin.title: Keys faked alike still join
testdataJoin.description: An order's customer_id and the customer's id are both faked as a hash. One real value always gives the same fake, so an order still finds its customer when both are fake.

testdataProd.title: Production: the real rows
testdataProd.description: In prod, the environment a request naming none is served, the customers read as they are.

testdataToDev.title: Switch to dev
testdataToDev.description: dev and test are environments of the model: branches of it, as in git. Both are Test (fake) environments. Next, the header's switcher moves to dev; every read after it is served from there.

testdataDev.title: The same query in dev
testdataDev.description: The same statement, read in dev: every column is its fake, computed by the engine as it reads. Names, emails, cities and dates look real and are not. Nothing was copied out of production.

testdataDevAnswer.title: Views and joins work on the fakes
testdataDevAnswer.description: A view joining orders, their lines, customers and products answers in dev too. Grouping, joining and adding up all run on the fakes, so a test exercises the same queries production runs.

testdataDevGraphql.title: Over GraphQL as well
testdataDevGraphql.description: Each order with the customer who placed it, through the relationship. Every API reads the environment it is served from, so a test suite against GraphQL, REST or SQL sees the same generated data.

testdataToTest.title: Switch to test
testdataToTest.description: Next, the switcher moves to test, the second Test (fake) environment.

testdataTest.title: The same fakes in test
testdataTest.description: A real value shows the same fake wherever it is read, so dev and test agree: a test written in dev finds the same rows in test.

testdataToProd.title: Back to production
testdataToProd.description: Next, the switcher returns to prod.

testdataProdAnswer.title: The real answer, in production only
testdataProdAnswer.description: The same view, read in prod: the real revenue by region and category. Only prod is served real rows; dev and test never see them.

testdataDone.title: What this is
testdataDone.description: Environments are branches of one model, and a fake is declared once per column. A Test (fake) environment answers every query with realistic generated values, keeps keys joinable, and is refused while a personal-data column has no fake. Production data never leaves production.

streamingScenario.title: Orders, live
streamingScenario.description: A coffee shop's orders arrive on a Kafka topic, a few a second, and its catalog is in its Postgres. The question: which regions placed the most orders in the last five minutes? orders is the broker the orders arrive on.

streamingJoin.title: Orders priced from the catalog
streamingJoin.description: PLACED_IN joins each order to its region, and ORDERED to its product, so an order's revenue comes from the catalog's price.

streamingAnswer.title: The busiest regions, now
streamingAnswer.description: orders_last_five_minutes is a materialized view: each region's orders and revenue in the last five minutes. Every batch of orders that lands refreshes it, so this read is of stored rows a few seconds old, never of the topic. Run it again in a minute and the numbers have moved.

streamingRecap.title: What you saw
streamingRecap.description: A Kafka topic landed as a table and joined to a live catalog; a view kept current by every batch that lands; the same answer in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached on request; and a subscription that moves with the feed. Look around on your own from the query page.

streamingCatalog.title: The catalog
streamingCatalog.description: catalog is the shop's Postgres, read live: what each product is and costs, and the regions the shop sells in.

streamingOrders.title: A topic becomes a table
streamingOrders.description: orders is the topic, landed into a table of its own as the orders arrive: a batch at most every two seconds, each order by its id. Every batch that lands refreshes the views that read it, and tells its subscribers.

streamingFresh.title: The orders as they land
streamingFresh.description: The latest orders in the table, a few seconds behind the topic. Each sandbox lands the whole topic into its own table, under its own consumer group.

streamingCached.title: The answer in GraphQL, cached
streamingCached.description: The same view in GraphQL. @cached(ttl: 10) asks for the response cache: the same question within ten seconds is answered from the cache, and the X-Provisa-Cache header says HIT.

streamingLive.title: Watch the orders arrive
streamingLive.description: A GraphQL subscription on the orders: every batch that lands sends the latest orders again, as it lands. Leave it running and watch the list move.

streamingRest.title: The answer over REST
streamingRest.description: The same view as a REST call, for a dashboard that polls it.

profilingScenario.title: What this demo is
profilingScenario.description: An outdoor retailer has bought a smaller one, Harbor Outfitters, and received its CRM's customers and orders. Before anyone builds on them, the question is: what is actually in this data? Provisa's built-in Data Profiler answers it, and its results are governed tables like any other, read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

profilingProfiler.title: The Data Profiler
profilingProfiler.description: A profiler holds a schedule and its run settings, nothing else: this one runs every night at 02:00. Its first run was made when the demo was built, so the results are already here.

profilingMember.title: A table joins the profiler
profilingMember.description: The customers and orders tables are members of the profiler. From a member's editor you can run a profile at once or view its runs: each run, its rows and how long it took.

profilingRuns.title: Each run is kept
profilingRuns.description: A run's results land as tables of their own, one for each kind of measure, and every run is kept beside the ones before it. Here are the customers table's runs, with the rows each read and the repeated rows it found.

profilingTerms.title: The vocabulary
profilingTerms.description: Data profile, plausible type, value shape, duplicate row and placeholder value, in the glossary, each tied to the measures it is about.

profilingAnswer.title: What each column holds
profilingAnswer.description: The view customer_columns keeps each customers column as the latest run found it, emptiest first. A fifth of the customers never answered the marketing question; some emails are missing and some hold a name instead; signup dates start at a 1900-01-01 placeholder, and lifetime values run from refunds below zero to test accounts at 999,999.99.

profilingTypes.title: What each column plausibly holds
profilingTypes.description: The profile infers what a column holds from its values, its name and its tags: an email, a phone number, a postal code, an identifier. Each comes with its confidence and the evidence for it.

profilingPhones.title: One column, four formats
profilingPhones.description: Each phone number reduced to its shape: a digit becomes 9. The CRM never checked the format, so one column holds four of them, which a join or a dialer would have to reconcile first.

profilingCountries.title: One country, several spellings
profilingCountries.description: The five commonest values of the country column: US, USA and United States are one country, written three ways among them alone. A count by country would split it.

profilingDuplicates.title: The rows written twice
profilingDuplicates.description: The model declares customer_id the key, but the export held no constraint: 150 customers are in it twice, every field the same. The profile counts the repeated rows and the key values held by more than one row.

profilingRest.title: The same answer over REST
profilingRest.description: The view is a REST endpoint too. A data quality tool or a migration script gets the profile without writing SQL.

profilingRecap.title: What you saw
profilingRecap.description: The acquired tables, read live, and a profile of them made by the built-in profiler and kept as governed tables: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, each answering what is actually in this data, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, under each role's access.

opioidsScenario.title: What this demo is
opioidsScenario.description: A state opioid settlement fund pays Ohio's 88 counties for treatment, recovery, prevention and naloxone. The council asks which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment the money pays for. The fund's allocations are in its own database; deaths, population and federal spending are public. The fund and its figures are made up; the counties and the public data are real.

opioidsJoin.title: Joined by county
opioidsJoin.description: The fund's counties and the public tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.

opioidsAnswer.title: The answer in SQL
opioidsAnswer.description: The view overdose_burden_by_county joins the fund's treatment and recovery spending to each county's deaths, and is kept stored. Ordered by deaths for each million dollars spent, it puts the counties where the money meets the most deaths first.

opioidsRecap.title: What you saw
opioidsRecap.description: The fund's own records, read live, and public health and census data, landed once, joined by county in one governed model. One stored view answers the council's question in SQL, GraphQL and REST, with staff and the public each seeing what their role allows.

opioidsGovdata.title: The public data
opioidsGovdata.description: The government data comes from AskAmerica, a live account: CDC's overdose deaths and death rates, the Census Bureau's population and USAspending's federal spending, each by county. Only Ohio's counties and 2023 are landed, once, when the demo is built, and read from that copy for good. 2023 is the year all of them cover.

opioidsAllocations.title: The fund's allocations
opioidsAllocations.description: Every allocation the fund made, read live from its own database: the county, the fiscal year, the program area, the provider paid, what was awarded and what has been spent. Staff see every row; the public role sees none.

opioidsDeaths.title: CDC's overdose death rates
opioidsDeaths.description: Overdose deaths per 100,000 residents in each county in 2023. Where a county had 1 to 9 deaths, CDC suppresses the count and publishes a modelled rate instead, flagged here, so every county has a rate to compare.

opioidsTerms.title: In plain words
opioidsTerms.description: The glossary explains the terms a council member or a resident meets: settlement fund, abatement, allocation, expenditure, suppressed count, rate per 100,000. Here abatement: what the settlements require the money be spent on.

opioidsAsPublic.title: Run as the public
opioidsAsPublic.description: The SQL explorer now runs as the public role, the role the council's dashboard and residents use. The statements that follow see only what it allows.

opioidsPublic.title: As the public sees it
opioidsPublic.description: The same view, run as the public role: the council's dashboard. It shows deaths, rates and spending per resident by county, and none of the fund's allocations or the providers paid.

opioidsByRegion.title: By region, in GraphQL
opioidsByRegion.description: The dashboard grouped by the fund's five regions: how many residents each has, and how much treatment and recovery was spent there.

opioidsRest.title: The same answer over REST
opioidsRest.description: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server, so a council website or a spreadsheet can read the dashboard over HTTP.

datavaultScenario.title: Two systems, one question
datavaultScenario.description: An order system and a CRM, both from Northwind, both with their own copy of each customer. The question: what did we know about this customer, from which source, and when? A data vault answers it by keeping every version from every source. Here the vault is declared as views, and the engine builds and refreshes it: no ETL platform, job server or pipeline code to run, the work runs on the engine where it scales, and one declared vault feeds the marts, the governed APIs and the lineage.

datavaultCrm.title: The CRM's own copy
datavaultCrm.description: The CRM holds the same customers as accounts, with each contact's email, which the order system never had. Its addresses can differ from the order system's, and for a while they do.

datavaultInsertOnly.title: Every row kept
datavaultInsertOnly.description: The customer table is insert-only, as a vault's staging receives it: a change arrives as a new row with its load date, and nothing is overwritten. The table watches its latest load date, so new rows refresh every view over it through the view cascade.

datavaultArrived.title: What arrived
datavaultArrived.description: Every row either system received for Alfreds Futterkiste. The order system heard of its move on 1 September 1997; the CRM sent the old address again on 1 October, and the move on 15 November.

datavaultHub.title: A hub
datavaultHub.description: One row per customer either system knows: its code, the hash key of the code that every link and satellite joins on, the system it was first seen in, and when.

datavaultLinks.title: Hub, link, hub
datavaultLinks.description: Links pair the hubs' hash keys: a customer placed an order, an order contains a product. The relationships between them let GraphQL and Cypher walk the vault from hub to link to hub.

datavaultSatellites.title: Satellites keep every version
datavaultSatellites.description: Each system's attributes for the customer, every version a row with its load date and a hashdiff over its values. The CRM's resend on 1 October has the hashdiff of the row before it, so it is no version.

datavaultProduct.title: A renamed product, a corrected price
datavaultProduct.description: The product satellite keeps Chai's old name beside Chai Tea, and Chang's price before and after its correction.

datavaultAnswer.title: What was known, and when
datavaultAnswer.description: The answer in one point-in-time query. At each date anything was loaded about the customer, the version of each system's values in force then, and since when. From 1 September to 15 November the two systems disagreed about where the customer lived.

datavaultGraphql.title: The same answer in GraphQL
datavaultGraphql.description: The business vault view is a GraphQL field too, filtered to the customer and ordered by time.

datavaultWalk.title: The vault walked in GraphQL
datavaultWalk.description: Hub to link to hub: the customer, its orders, the products in them, and every version of each product's name and price.

datavaultRest.title: The mart over REST
datavaultRest.description: The current-state customer dimension, built on the vault, is a REST endpoint: a downstream application reads it without knowing the vault is there.

datavaultLineage.title: Where a mart column comes from
datavaultLineage.description: The lineage of the mart's columns: each one traced back through the point-in-time view and the satellites to the source field it came from.

datavaultAnalyst.title: An analyst's view
datavaultAnalyst.description: Next runs the SQL explorer as the European analyst. Personal data lives in the satellites, so that is where it is governed.

datavaultMasked.title: Masked where the personal data is
datavaultMasked.description: As the analyst, the CRM satellite shows only European customers, their contacts withheld, their email names and phone digits hidden. The hubs and links stay readable, so the analyst can still join on them.

datavaultRecap.title: What you saw
datavaultRecap.description: Two live systems and a data vault over them, declared as views: hubs, links and satellites with every version kept, refreshed by the engine as rows arrive, governed in the satellites, and queried point-in-time in SQL, GraphQL and REST, with lineage back to the source fields. No separate ETL platform, job server or pipeline code.

status.stuck: This step is taking longer than expected. The page may still be loading.

weblogs.title: The web shop's logs
weblogs.summary: A web shop's question, which pages are slow and which SQL makes them slow: its sources, the tables they become, the join of its two logs, and the answer in SQL and over REST.

sonnets.title: Shakespeare's sonnets
sonnets.summary: The 154 sonnets embedded, searched by meaning and grown into a graph: the themes they share and the lines where Shakespeare echoes himself.

files.title: Instant data lake
files.summary: A city's open-data files read in place as one catalog: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?

reviews.title: Product reviews
reviews.summary: An electronics shop's catalog, reviews and purchases in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Neo4j, joined on the product: which products do reviews say the battery dies on, and what else did their buyers buy?

insurance.title: Property exposure and hazard risk
insurance.summary: A property insurer's question, where its exposure is concentrated against hazard risk: its own policies joined by county to FEMA, wildfire and storm data, answered in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

quality.title: Data you can trust
quality.summary: A chain of shops' sales feed refined from bronze to silver and gold by checked materialized views: landing a batch is all it takes, and a batch that fails a check never reaches silver.

insider.title: Insider review
insider.summary: A bank's outbound mail matched against its watch list of deals in discussion and checked for customer data, ranked in one review queue that a first-level reviewer reads without ever seeing the list.

vulnerabilities.title: Exploited vulnerabilities in our code
vulnerabilities.summary: A software company's Dependabot alerts joined by CVE to the NVD and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities: which exploited vulnerabilities sit in our code, and how far past CISA's due date are they?

testdata.title: Test data
testdata.summary: A shop's production database, read in prod as it is and in two test environments as realistic generated data, the same queries and joins answering in all three.

streaming.title: Live order stream
streaming.summary: A coffee shop's orders arrive live on Kafka and are joined to its catalog: a view of the busiest regions in the last five minutes, refreshed by every batch that lands, answered in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached, and watched with a subscription.

profiling.title: What is actually in this data?
profiling.summary: An acquired company's customers and orders, profiled by the built-in Data Profiler: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, landed as governed tables and read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

opioids.title: Opioid settlement funds and overdose deaths
opioids.summary: A local government's question, which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment their opioid settlement money pays for: a fund's allocations joined by county to CDC, Census and federal spending data.

datavault.title: Data vault
datavault.summary: A data vault declared over an order system and a CRM: hubs, links and satellites the engine builds and refreshes as rows arrive, personal data masked in the satellites, and one point-in-time query for what was known about a customer, from which source, and when.
